slides.title: Market: growing, but unprofitable
US quick-commerce sales grew 2.8 times from 2022 to 2025, confirming the founders' view that demand is strong

claims.claim: US quick-commerce sales grew 2.8 times from 2022 to 2025
evidence: 2.8x growth in US quick-commerce sales from 2022 to 2025

claims.claim: Every year above 38%, in line with the founders' "over 40% a year"
evidence: sales grew 44% in 2023, 38% in 2024 and 42% in 2025

claims.claim: No slowdown yet: 2025 growth was faster than 2024 growth
Demand is not the question: whether any operator can serve it at a profit is

slides.title: Neither incumbent has turned that growth into profit, whether measured on each order or at the EBITDA line

claims.claim: The national leader loses a quarter of its revenue; the regional player nearly half
evidence: EBITDA margin 2025: Zipcart (national) -0.2583; QuickBasket (regional) -0.4571

claims.claim: Neither covers its costs on an order, before any head-office spending
evidence: Contribution per order 2025, $: Zipcart -1.9; QuickBasket -3.4

claims.claim: QuickBasket, the regional operator closest to our plan, closed 4 of its 11 cities in 2025

slides.title: Zipcart's one profitable city shows what profit costs: a new fee, almost no promotions and 14% fewer orders

claims.claim: The founders cite it as proof the model works
evidence: Zipcart lost $310M of EBITDA on $1,200M of revenue in 2025
Across its network, each order lost $1.90 in contribution
The densest city is the most favourable test case it has

claims.claim: Profit came from charging more and discounting less
evidence: Added a new $3.99 service fee on every order
Cut promotions to 1% of order value, against the benchmark's 6%
Accepted lower volume in the city to get there
$0.4 contribution per order in that city, Q4 2025
−14% change in the city's order volume afterwards

claims.claim: Our plan charges only the $1.99 delivery fee, so it cannot copy the route to profit that Zipcart took

slides.title: Unit economics
Only the founders' plan makes money per order; even the best inputs any site has reached lose $1.76 after store costs

claims.claim: Profit appears only in the plan
evidence: Contribution per order after dark-store costs, $: Founders' plan 2.0182; Best inputs observed -1.7572; Benchmark median -6.1666; Columbus pop-up -12.5725

claims.claim: Founders' plan: the only case above zero, and it needs four inputs better than the best site
Best inputs observed: the best value seen for each input, so it caps every one of the 14 sites; none makes money after store costs
Benchmark median: before store costs it loses $2.67, between Zipcart's $1.90 and QuickBasket's $3.40 losses
evidence: $11.2 goods margin plus fee − $13.8 order costs and promotions − $3.5 dark store per order = −$6.2 per order

claims.claim: Columbus pop-up: the lowest density, spread over a small temporary site

slides.title: The plan assumes four inputs better than any site has achieved, though no site has even combined the best two

claims.claim: Founders' plan inputs sit above the observed range
evidence: Benchmark median: $34; 2.4 orders per rider-hour; 900 orders per store a day; 6% promotions
Founders' plan: $45; 3.5; 1,800; 2% — Its 3.5 orders per rider-hour and 1,800 orders a day sit above the top of the benchmark range
Benchmark range: 1.9–3.0 orders per rider-hour and 400–1,400 orders per site a day

claims.claim: Best inputs observed: best value of each input; order value and density peaked at different sites
evidence: Best inputs observed: $42; 3; 1,400; 6%

claims.claim: Columbus pop-up: below the median on all four inputs
evidence: Columbus pop-up: $31; 2.1; 280; 12%

slides.title: Breaking even on an order, before store costs, would take an order worth about $47, more than any site has seen

claims.claim: Break-even order value before store costs is about $47
evidence: $11.8 per-order costs that do not grow with the basket: picking $3.10, rider $7.40, payment and packaging $1.30
− $1.99 delivery fee collected on each order
÷ 21% kept per dollar of order value: 27% goods margin less 6% promotions
= $46.7 order value at which an order breaks even, before store costs

claims.claim: Even the plan's $45 order falls short unless riders also beat the best site
evidence: Riders deliver the benchmark median of 2.4 orders an hour at $17.75 an hour
Promotions stay at the benchmark's 6% of order value; goods margin is 27% at every site
Store rent, staff and utilities are left out; covering them at 900 orders a day takes an order of about $63
The best observed site reached $42 and the pop-up $31

slides.title: Rider pay, the largest cost in every order, is the one that new minimum-pay rules in two launch cities would raise

claims.claim: Rider pay is the largest cost in every order
evidence: Cost per order, $, benchmark median 2025: Riders 7.3958; Dark store 3.5008; Picking and packing 3.1; Promotions 2.04; Payment and packaging 1.3; Money kept per order (goods margin + fee) 11.17
42.7% of the full cost of an order goes to the rider at median productivity
Riders: $17.75 an hour over 2.4 orders; at the best site's 3.0 orders an hour the cost falls to $5.92

claims.claim: Pay rules: 2 of the 3 launch cities are considering minimum pay for delivery workers, which can only push this line up
Dark store: falls only with density
evidence: at the pop-up's 280 orders a day a full store would cost $11.25 per order
store = $1.15M a year ÷ (900 orders × 365 days)

slides.title: Columbus pop-up test
Promotions at twice the benchmark rate explain almost half of the pop-up's extra loss on each order

claims.claim: 47.4% of the pop-up's extra loss per order comes from promotions
evidence: Loss per order before store costs, $: Benchmark median 2.6658; Lower order value +0.81; Higher promotions +1.68; Fewer orders per rider-hour +1.0565; Columbus pop-up 6.2124
Higher promotions: 12% of order value against the median's 6%; they bought the 18% weekly growth

claims.claim: Fewer orders per rider-hour: 2.1 against 2.4, as riders waited for scattered orders
Lower order value: $31 against $34, so each order carried less margin
Not shown: the temporary store added a further $6.36 per order at 280 orders a day
evidence: 11,800 orders over six weeks at one temporary site

slides.title: Real use falls well short of stated intent, with only 22% of pop-up customers still ordering in month three

claims.claim: What people say: survey of 1,500 residents
evidence: 44% of residents aged 25–39 said they would use it at least weekly
Asked of the age group most likely to use it, not of all residents
A stated intention, with no price or fee attached
The founders' demand case leans on this signal

claims.claim: What customers did: pop-up customer data
evidence: 22% of pop-up customers were still ordering in month three
Measured on real orders during the six-week test
Seen while promotions ran at 12% of order value
Retention may fall further once promotions are cut

claims.claim: Even loyal customers order less than weekly
evidence: 0.7 orders a week by those who stayed (3.1 a month)
Below the weekly habit the survey implies
Fewer orders per customer means more spend to fill each store
Density, the plan's key input, depends on this habit

slides.title: A pop-up customer who stays costs about $173 to win and takes 15 months to repay, even at the plan's margins

claims.claim: A customer who stays costs about $173 to win and takes 15 months to repay
evidence: $38 to acquire one customer through paid social and first-order credits ÷ 22% of customers still ordering in month three = $172.7 to acquire each customer who stays
÷ $11.7 a month from that customer: 3.1 orders × the plan's $3.77 per order = 14.8 months to earn back the cost

claims.claim: At benchmark or pop-up economics the cost is never earned back
evidence: The plan's $3.77 contribution per order before store costs; at the benchmark median each order loses $2.67
Customers who stay keep ordering 3.1 times a month with no further churn, which flatters the payback
After store costs ($2.02 per order on the plan) payback stretches to about 28 months
Acquisition cost stays at $38 once promotions and first-order credits are cut

slides.title: Cash and runway
Even if the plan works, it leaves $2.5M at month 18, about half the 12-month runway the board requires

claims.claim: The plan leaves $2.5M at month 18
evidence: Cash $M: Cash today 12; Store capex −5.4; Launch marketing and operating losses −4.1; Cash at month 18 2.5
Store capex: $0.6M a store, spent before any store proves itself

claims.claim: 6.2 months of runway left at month 18 at today's burn of $0.4M a month, against a floor of 12
If the $9.5M excludes today's burn: $7.2M more goes, and cash runs out first
The floor needs $4.8M at today's burn; the plan fails it on its own numbers

slides.title: At benchmark-median economics, nine full stores would lose about $18M a year, one and a half times our cash

claims.claim: Nine full stores would lose about $18M a year, 1.5x our cash
evidence: 9 dark stores × 328,500 orders a year per store at the median of 900 a day × −$6.2 contribution per order after store costs = −$18.2M a year, before launch marketing and head-office costs
÷ $12M cash in the bank today = 1.5x the bank balance, lost every year

claims.claim: The upside exists only if every plan input beats the best site
evidence: All nine stores run at full volume for a whole year, with no ramp-up, launch marketing or head-office cost
At the best inputs observed (1,400 orders a day, $42 orders) the network still loses about $8M a year
Only on the founders' plan inputs (1,800 orders a day, $45 orders) does it earn about $12M a year
Every case uses $1.15M a year per store and the per-order costs of Table 3

slides.title: Scaling the software is the better use of cash; revisit operating once three conditions hold
Scaling the software is the one option that protects the runway floor and builds on what grocers already ask for

claims.claim: Launch Parcelbird Now: Reject: breaks the runway floor on plan numbers and competes with our customers
evidence: Runway: the launch leaves about 6 months at month 18 (p. 17)
Economics: no benchmark site can make money per order after store costs (p. 8)

claims.claim: Test one permanent dark store first: Not now: repeats the pop-up at a higher cost, and median stores lose on every order
evidence: One test store at median economics loses about $2.0M a year (328,500 orders × −$6.17), taking runway below 12 months within about 8 months

claims.claim: Scale the software for grocers: Recommended / Positive margin from the first contract, and it helps grocers launch fast delivery from their own stores
evidence: Grocer fit: briefing pack §10

slides.title: Scaling the software pays for itself once about 10 new grocers sign, and the late-stage pipeline alone nearly gets there

claims.claim: 10.3 new contracts pay for the 2 engineers and 2 sales hires
evidence: $0.8M ÷ ($96,000 contract × 81% gross margin) = 10.3
Hires cost $0.8M a year, against $9.5M for the launch
With no new contract, runway falls only from 30 to 26 months

claims.claim: $0.9M of ARR if the 9 late-stage grocers sign
evidence: 21% on top of today's $4.1M ARR
Their gross profit covers 87% of the hiring cost
On top of ARR already growing 60% a year

claims.claim: $3.6M of ARR if all 37 pipeline grocers sign
evidence: 87% of today's ARR
Several want fast delivery from their own stores, which our software runs
As an operator we would become their competitor

claims.claim: Growth through software needs $0.8M a year and no new funding round, compared with $9.5M for the launch

slides.title: The board can reopen the operator question once three conditions hold, and none of them holds today

claims.claim: Condition 1: A site in our software network makes money on each order after store costs, with high order value and density at the same site
evidence: 14 benchmark sites; even their best inputs lose money after store costs

claims.claim: Condition 2: Rider pay rules are settled in Columbus, Indianapolis and Kansas City, so the largest cost line is known
evidence: 2 of the three launch cities are considering minimum pay for riders

claims.claim: Condition 3: Funding covers the launch and still keeps 12 months of runway, without a new round
evidence: $14.3M needed for the plan plus the floor, $2.3M more than the $12.0M in the bank
Condition 3 uses the plan's $9.5M plus 12 months of today's $0.4M burn ($4.8M)

claims.claim: Ask the founders to bring the case back when a site in our network makes money after store costs

slides.title: Next steps

normalized.recommendation: Do not launch Parcelbird Now in 2027; scale the software for grocers instead (hire 2 engineers and 2 sales hires at $0.8M a year); revisit operating once three conditions hold — ask the founders to bring the case back when a site in our network makes money after store costs.

alternatives_considered.option: Launch Parcelbird Now: nine dark stores
alternatives_considered.treatment: Reject: breaks the runway floor on plan numbers and competes with our customers

alternatives_considered.option: Test one permanent dark store first
alternatives_considered.treatment: Not now: repeats the pop-up at a higher cost, and median stores lose on every order; one test store at median economics loses about $2.0M a year, taking runway below 12 months within about 8 months
Recommended: positive margin from the first contract, and it helps grocers launch fast delivery from their own stores

assumptions_and_uncertainties: Fictional company; synthetic benchmark data from the briefing pack
The pack does not define the operators' contribution per order
Pop-up costs not measured in the test taken at benchmark
Best inputs observed = best value seen for each input, not one site
Break-even: riders deliver the benchmark median of 2.4 orders an hour at $17.75 an hour; promotions stay at 6%; goods margin is 27% at every site; store rent, staff and utilities are left out
Pop-up: goods margin, delivery fee, picking and payment costs taken at benchmark; 11,800 orders over six weeks at one temporary site
Survey and customer data use different groups, so they show direction, not an exact gap
Retention may fall further once promotions are cut
Payback assumes customers who stay keep ordering 3.1 times a month with no further churn, which flatters the payback; acquisition cost stays at $38 once promotions and first-order credits are cut

The pack does not say whether the $9.5M includes the software business's own burn, so the chart uses the reading most favourable to the plan; if it excludes today's burn, $7.2M more goes and cash runs out first
Nine-store estimate assumes all stores run at full volume for a whole year, with no ramp-up, launch marketing or head-office cost; $1.15M a year per store
Contract values at the pipeline average of $96,000 a year; the pack gives no conversion rates
2 of the 3 launch cities are considering minimum pay for delivery workers, which can only push rider cost up
next_steps: Decline the Parcelbird Now launch and confirm the 12-month runway floor — Board — January 2027
Hire 2 engineers and 2 sales staff; work the 9 late-stage grocers to signature — CEO — Q1 2027
Package fast delivery from existing stores as a software offer for pipeline grocers — Founders — Q1–Q2 2027
Report contribution after store costs for every customer site, as the trigger to revisit — Finance lead — Quarterly from Q2 2027
Track minimum-pay rules for riders in the three cities — Operations lead — Ongoing
